fixes.explanation: Wail is the word, friend. Isaiah opens with “Wail, O ships of Tarshish…” (Isaiah 23:1). The news is so heavy that even the ships get told to cry out. I think that's about the saddest way you could start a message.

This one sounds like a locked front door, but that's not what Isaiah says. He never says Tyre shut its harbor to the ships. Tyre is laid waste, “…without house or harbor.” A closed door can be opened again, friend, but that's not the picture here.

True, friend. The verse says word has reached them from the land of Cyprus. So the news about Tyre comes to the ships of Tarshish from Cyprus. That's a detail that's easy to slide past, and you caught it.

Merchant is right. Isaiah says Tyre “…was the merchant of the nations.” (Isaiah 23:3). Grain from the Nile came across the water, and its harvest was Tyre's revenue. Merchant is the title the verse gives her.

That's what Isaiah says. “When the report reaches Egypt, they will writhe in agony over the news of Tyre.” (Isaiah 23:5). The verse gives us their reaction, and it's a strong word. Egypt is also the land of the Nile harvest that Isaiah just said was Tyre's revenue (Isaiah 23:3).

That sounds like a kind neighbor, but Isaiah doesn't say it. He says Egypt will writhe in agony over the news of Tyre. The verse gives their reaction and nothing about any rescue fleet. Stick with what the text gives, baker.

Isaiah doesn't say the harbor goes to Sidon. He tells Sidon to be ashamed (Isaiah 23:4). The reason the verse gives is “…to disgrace all the renowned of the earth.” That's the answer on the card, friend.

Right, and the verse says it plainly: “there is no longer a harbor.” (Isaiah 23:10). So the Daughter of Tarshish is told to cultivate her land like the Nile. The harbor is the reason Isaiah gives. That's the whole answer, friend.
The verse compares her land to the Nile, but Isaiah never says anyone wants to buy her crops. The stated reason is “there is no longer a harbor.” Don't go adding customers, friend.
